title: Design a Personal Blog
brief: A hobbyist writes a blog about hiking trips. Each visit is a request: a server builds the page from posts kept in a database. On most days the blog is quiet. Now and then a post is shared on a big news site and, for a few hours, far more people arrive than usual. Visitors should still get their page, even if one of your servers has a bad day, and the monthly bill should stay small.
constraints: A page must load within 300 ms on a normal day
About 100 page views per second on a normal day
When a post is shared, traffic can reach about 12 times that for a few hours
The blog keeps working if one server fails

scenarios.title: Normal day
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Follow one page view from the visitor to the database and back. Which block is busiest on a normal day, and how do you know?
scenarios.debrief: On a normal day the whole blog uses a small share of its capacity, so any sensible design passes. The scenarios that follow are what separate designs.

scenarios.title: Shared on a news site (12x)
scenarios.description: A post is shared and traffic jumps to twelve times normal for a few hours.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Traffic is twelve times higher. Which block fills up first, and what are your two options for coping?
scenarios.debrief: Twelve times normal is more than one default-sized server can answer, so something has to give: more capacity in one place, or the same work shared between copies.

scenarios.title: A server fails
scenarios.description: One of the servers stops working on an ordinary day.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: One server stops at an ordinary moment. What does a visitor see in your design?
scenarios.debrief: A design that depends on a single server has nothing left to answer when it fails. Spare capacity kept in a second copy is what lets the blog carry on.

requirements.text: Pages load within the latency target on a normal day
At least 98% of visitors are served when a post is shared
The blog keeps working when one server fails
A server builds each page from posts kept in a database

rubric: A server receives each request and reads the posts it needs from a database.
The design has enough capacity for the shared-post surge without paying for that capacity all month if it can avoid it.
More than one copy of the server runs, so a single failure does not take the blog down.
The design says which block would fill up first if traffic grew further.

reference.summary: Share the work between a few identical servers behind a load balancer, with enough spare room that losing one still leaves the blog standing.
design: User, then a Load Balancer, then a Server running 'the page' with three replicas of 500 requests a second each.
The Server reads posts from a Database sized for the shared-post peak.
tradeoffs: Three smaller copies cost about the same as two large ones, but losing one leaves a bigger share of capacity behind.
The database is still a single copy. The design passes every scenario here, but it would not survive that database failing; later lessons cover that.
